9. Voice

NCode writes the way one engineer tells another exactly what a thing does, in the order they need it, and what it costs. The same voice runs through a README, a decision record, an error message and a landing page.

How NCode Writes

  1. Say what it does, with the mechanism, in the first sentence. "Pinned, pooled .NET buffers that zero themselves on dispose, for keys and other secrets." No adjective in it is a claim: each is a property the code has.
  2. Give the reason in the same sentence as the rule. "Never put it in a public issue: that tells attackers about it before a fix exists."
  3. Use exact numbers and names. "128 by 128, the size NuGet recommends." "NCode Blue on a dark page is 2.1 to 1, too low to read: use the light mark or a tile there."
  4. State limits and costs as plainly as features. "Nothing here is pinned or zeroed." "It starts no threads, performs no I/O and opens no network connection."
  5. Title a decision with the decision. "A person merges every pull request." A heading is a sentence someone can disagree with.
  6. Address the reader as "you", in the imperative, in the present tense. "Pick the row that matches your data."
  7. Tables for choices, prose for reasons. Facts every row shares go in the sentence above the table.
  8. Be direct and civil about what was rejected. Say why, once, without scorn.

Do and Don't

DoDon't
"Each of these zeroes its memory on dispose.""Enterprise-grade memory security you can trust."
"Report a vulnerability in NCode.Buffers privately.""We take security very seriously."
"The mark sits at one of three sizes in its square.""Our logo is carefully crafted to look great everywhere."
"A larger buffer gets its own pinned array, still zeroed on dispose.""Seamlessly handles buffers of any size."
"Keep the lockup at least 24 pixels high.""Please try to avoid making the logo too small!"
"The script runs on the Node.js release .node-version names, with no packages to install.""Simply run our easy build script."
  • No superlatives and no unprovable adjectives: not "blazing", "robust", "seamless", "powerful", "best-in-class", "simply", "just" or "easy". If a property matters, state the measurement.
  • No exclamation marks, no emoji and no rhetorical questions.
  • Name the thing: the type, the file, the command, the size, the ratio, the decision record.
  • Say what something does not do when a reader might assume it does.
  • One idea per sentence, with a colon before the reason or the consequence. When a sentence needs a second colon, split it.

In an Interface

  • A key says what it does: "Create client", "Rotate secret". Sentence case, no ellipsis unless it opens a dialog that asks for more.
  • An error says what happened and what to do: "The username or password is incorrect." Never "Oops".
  • A destructive action names its object and its consequence: "Delete client billing-service. Tokens it holds stop working."
  • An empty state says what would be here and how to add it: "No clients yet. Create one to request tokens."
  • A name is engraved, a value is displayed: a narrow uppercase label names a part, and a monospace value is read off the system. Don't write a value in the label voice or a label in the value voice.

A product or landing page keeps the same voice. Its first line is the README's first line: what it is and the property that matters. Proof, such as a number, a standard or a signed release, replaces praise.
